text: You are born with a blood clot clenched in your fist. The midwives freeze.
The old men whisper that it is a sign that this boy will command men.
But a sign promises nothing.
By the time you are nine, your father will be poisoned.
Your own tribe will abandon your family to die on the steppe.
At sixteen, you will walk through an enemy camp with a wooden board locked around your neck
and anyone will be free to strike you.
And from that position, you will build the largest land empire in history. Here is how.
The year is around 1162.
You are born by the Onon River.
At the edge of a world no one is writing books about yet. There are no kings here. No cities. No laws.
Only pastures, horse herds, and tribes that have been slaughtering each other for generations over every stream.
Your father's name is Yesuge.
He is the leader of a small clan.
A warrior and a raider with far too many enemies.
On the very day you are born, he returns from a raid with a captured tatar named Temujin.
So that is the name you are given.
It is not yet Genghis Khan.
That name you will have to earn.
And the price will be enormous.
You are taught what the steppe demands.
At five, you ride.
At six, you shoot a small bow.
You know what a coming blizzard smells like.
You know how horses behave when wolves are near.
You cannot read because your people have no writing.
But you know how to listen.
And that will matter more.
When you turn nine, your father takes you on a journey.
He wants to find you a bride from another tribe.
On the steppe, alliances were made this way.
Children were betrothed early so that blood would bind clans tighter than promises.
On the road, you meet a family you like.
The girl's name is Borte. She is older than you.
She looks you straight in the eye and she is not afraid.
Your father leaves you with her family as a pledge and rides home alone.
It is the last time you will see him.
On his way back, your father stops at a stranger's fire.
Tatars sit around it, his old enemies.
But the law of the steppe is strong.
A guest must never be harmed.
A guest must be fed.
They feed him, smiling.
And they poison the food.
Yesuge makes it home, but he is already dying.
He manages to send for you.
You ride across the entire steppe, but you arrive too late.
You stand over your father's body and you are nine years old.
But the worst is still ahead.
You assume the tribe will protect you, but all they see is this.
The leader is dead and his sons are too young to lead warriors.
No one wants to feed a widow and her children.
One morning, you wake up and the camp is empty.
The people left in the night and took the herds with them.
You, your mother, and your brothers are alone. No one offers help. No one comes back.
You learn the first truth of your life.
A word means nothing without strength behind it.
For the next years, you live like an animal. You dig for roots.
You catch fish in freezing rivers.
You hunt marmots and mice.
Your mother teaches you patience.
One day, she snaps a single arrow shaft in front of you. Easy.
Then she takes a bundle of shafts and hands it to you. Try. No one can break it.
You are strong, she says, only while you stand together.
But even this family has a crack in it.
Your half -brother, Bektor, steals your food and insists he is the eldest.
You endure it for a long time.
Then you walk out into the step with your brother and together you kill Bektor.
Your mother is furious.
She calls you murderers, but you understand what she refuses to admit.
In a world where the weak are abandoned, a family either survives as one or dies piece by piece.
It is your first blood.
It will not be your last.
But you are not cruel by nature.
You are simply learning that the world does not forgive weakness.
And while you are learning it, someone is already watching you.
Your father's enemies fear you.
They remember that a boy grows and that a wolf cub becomes a wolf.
They decide to remove you before you get strong.
You are about 16. They catch you.
They lock a wooden collar around your neck, heavy as a door. You cannot eat properly. You cannot lie down.
You cannot even brush away a fly.
They drag you from tent to tent and anyone has the right to humiliate you. But you do not beg. You watch.
You count the guard's steps.
You remember who drinks and who doesn't.
On the night of a great feast, you are guarded by a weak young man.
You swing the collar into his head and run.
The camp wakes up and men chase you with torches.
You dive into the river and lie on the bottom, leaving only your face above the water.
A man from the enemy clan spots you.
His name is Sorganshira. He could shout.
Instead, he says nothing.
Then he hides you in a cart full of wool and saves your life. Remember this lesson.
You did not survive because you were stronger.
You survived because the people around you chose to help you.
Power is not built on fear.
It is built on people wanting to follow you.
You go back for Borte and you marry her.
You are happy, but not for long.
One dawn, the Merkits attack your camp.
They have wanted revenge on your clan for years.
They take the one thing most precious to you and they carry your wife away. You have no army.
You have a handful of men and one old friend of your father's.
Togrul, the Khan of the Karaites.
You ride to him with gifts and he agrees to help.
Your sworn brother Jamuka joins you, a friend from childhood with whom you once exchanged oaths.
Together, you attack the Merkits at night.
You burst into the camp, shouting your wife's name.
In the darkness, she hears you and runs toward your voice.
But sometime later, Borte gives birth to a son and no one knows whose child he is.
You accept him as your own and you name him Jochi.
Many whisper that you are weak. You do not answer them.
You have already understood.
Real strength is not in answering everyone.
Over the years, people are drawn to you.
Not because you are noble, but because beside you, a simple herdsman can become a commander.
You value skill, not bloodline.
You divide the spoils fairly.
You remember the name of every man who served you.
But the nobles hate this.
And the first to grow unhappy is Jamuka, your sworn brother.
He believes in the old order.
Power belongs to those born noble.
You believe in a new one.
Power belongs to those who earn it.
This is not just an argument.
It is a fight over what kind of world will exist.
One day, you split your camps.
You part without a quarrel, but both of you know you will meet again.
And next time, it will be on the battlefield.
He will become your greatest enemy.
You will defeat him, and he will return.
He will beat you once, and you will survive only by luck.
But in the end, you will capture him.
You will offer him a place at your side, as it once was. He will refuse.
He will ask for only one thing, to die without his blood being spilled.
You will grant his request. You lost a friend.
But you stayed true to what you believed.
For the next 20 years, you fight.
You crush the Tatars, the poisoners of your father. You defeat the Merkits. You conquer the Naimans.
Even Togru, your old protector, becomes your enemy.
And you must defeat him, too.
You do what no one before you has done.
You break the old system.
Tribes stop being the main unit of society.
Your army is divided into tens, hundreds, and thousands.
And commanders are chosen for merit, not birth.
Betrayal is punished by death.
Plunder is shared fairly.
A promise is kept.
You establish a code of rules that will later be known as the Yasa.
It is simple and harsh, but it applies to everyone equally.
In the year 1206,
the leaders of all the tribes gather at a great assembly near the source of the Onan,
the very place where you were born.
Above the steppe, they raise a white banner with nine tails.
They proclaim you Genghis Khan.
It means universal ruler or ruler of the oceans.
You are 44 years old.
Behind you, the wooden collar, the hunger, the betrayals.
Ahead of you, the whole world.
You do not want war with the Shah of Khwarezm. You want trade.
You send a caravan loaded with goods and envoys carrying an offer of peace.
But the governor of a border city orders the merchants killed and their goods seized.
You send new envoys and demand that the guilty man be handed over.
The Shah kills your envoys too.
And now, this is no longer just an insult.
To you, it is a broken treaty.
And you consider a treaty sacred.
In 1219, you march.
Your army is organized better than any in the world.
It has scouts who know the roads before the troops ever reach them. It has communication.
Riders carry news for hundreds of miles faster than an enemy can prepare.
It has a discipline no one else possesses.
Cities that surrender live.
Cities that resist vanish.
The news runs ahead of you. Fear becomes your weapon.
And often, a fortress opens its gates without a single arrow fired.
But you do not only destroy. You build.
You create a relay system where messengers ride day and night. You protect merchants.
You allow every faith because what matters to you is not prayer but loyalty.
You bring in scholars and scribes because your own people have no writing and you quickly understand its power.
Your empire is brutal.
But a merchant can cross it with gold through half the world and arrive safe.
That is the paradox of your power.
You destroy those who resist and you protect those who submit.
You are about 65 now, an old man.
Your body is worn down by decades of campaigns. But you cannot stop.
In 1227, you lead your army against the Tanguts who broke their word.
During the campaign, you fall from your horse and you never fully recover.
What exactly killed you no one knows because the chroniclers tell it differently.
You want your death kept secret until the war is over.
You are buried in secret.
The location remains unknown.
According to legend, everyone who saw the road was killed.
According to legend, a herd of horses was driven over the grave to erase every trace.
To this day, no one knows where you lie.
But your empire lives on.
It will stretch from the Pacific Ocean to the Caspian Sea and beyond.
Your sons and grandsons will rule half the known world.
Within a few generations, you will be the ancestor of millions.
And it all began with a boy whose father was murdered and who was left on the step to die.
Now, a question for you. Would you have survived?
At which moment would you have broken? The wooden collar? Losing Borte?
Or the betrayal of your closest friend? Tell me in the comments.
And in the next video, you will be born in ancient Rome.
And the arena is waiting for you.
